sonnet.problem: The card says Job is "a man who has lost nearly everything." That is a fact from outside the passage, and it has no reference in brackets. It is more than a short who-someone-is label.
sonnet.rule: A fact from outside it gives its reference in brackets in the card's text, like "Jeremiah, a prophet (Jeremiah 1:5)." A short label saying who someone is, like "Moses, Israel's leader," needs no reference.

sonnet.problem: The card asks what the windblown leaf and dry chaff picture says about Job himself, and marks "He's weak and helpless" as correct. Job 13:25 only asks two questions and never says what the picture stands for.
sonnet.rule: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect. This includes what a picture means. He retells the picture as the text gives it and says what it stands for only when the passage says so.

sonnet.problem: The card tells nothing from Job 14:2. It only says Job grabs a picture "anybody can see just by stepping outside," which adds a setting and a purpose the text doesn't give. It moves nothing forward.
sonnet.rule: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. ... Every story card tells part of the passage.

sonnet.problem: The card jokes (a fresh batch on the cooling rack, gone the second he turns his back) about the fleeting shadow of a man's life. Job 14:2 is about how short and fragile human life is, which is the heavy topic of death, so the card should have no joke.
sonnet.rule: A card that tells death, violence, abuse, serious sin or the body's private matters has no joke.
